chapters.title: From the ancient to the modern world

points.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
points.brief: Invasions, weak rulers and money troubles ended Roman rule in western Europe in 476 CE, while the Eastern Empire, Byzantium, lasted another thousand years.

points.title: Christianity in medieval Europe
points.brief: The Catholic Church, led by the Pope, shaped daily life, learning and politics across western Europe, and was rich from the taxes and land it held.

points.title: The rise of Islam
points.brief: Islam began in Arabia in the 7th century with the prophet Muhammad and spread quickly. Scholars in cities such as Baghdad kept and advanced learning in science, maths and medicine.

points.title: Trade routes across the world
points.brief: The Silk Road and sea routes carried silk, spices, ideas and also disease between China, India, the Islamic world and Europe.

points.title: Voyages of discovery
points.brief: From the late 1400s, European sailors such as Columbus and da Gama sought sea routes to Asia's riches, reaching the Americas and India and starting a new age of contact and conquest.

points.title: Comparing sources to check accuracy
points.brief: When two sources made independently agree, each is more likely to be accurate. When they disagree, the historian looks for why.

points.title: Bias and reliability
points.brief: A biased source shows one side, often because of who made it and why, such as a monk writing about Viking raids. Knowing the bias helps judge how reliable it is.

points.title: Historical empathy
points.brief: Empathy in history means understanding why people acted as they did by their own beliefs and conditions, without judging them only by today's values.

points.title: Judging historical significance
points.brief: An event or person is significant if it affected many people, had lasting effects or changed how people lived and thought, such as the printing press.

points.title: Writing a historical explanation
points.brief: A good explanation opens with a clear point, backs it with evidence from sources, explains how the evidence supports the point, and links it to the question.

points.title: Feudalism
points.brief: Under feudalism the king granted land to lords in return for loyalty and soldiers, and lords gave land to knights, with peasants working it at the bottom.

points.title: Life on the manor
points.brief: Most people were peasants on a lord's manor. Serfs could not leave the land, worked the lord's fields and paid him part of their crops.

points.title: Knights, castles and chivalry
points.brief: Knights trained for years to fight on horseback and followed a code of chivalry. Castles protected lords and showed their power over the land around them.

points.title: The power of the Church
points.brief: The Church collected a tithe, a tenth of what people produced, ran monasteries that copied books and cared for the sick, and could cast people out of the Church.

points.title: Medieval law and punishment
points.brief: Guilt was often decided by trial by ordeal or by combat, in the belief that God would protect the innocent, and punishments were public and harsh.

points.title: The Crusades
points.brief: From 1095, Christian armies from Europe fought Muslim rulers for control of Jerusalem. The wars brought death on both sides but also new trade and ideas to Europe.

points.title: The Black Death arrives
points.brief: Plague reached Europe in 1347 along trade routes, spread by fleas on rats and from person to person, and killed about a third of Europe's people in a few years.

points.title: Effects of the Black Death
points.brief: With so many workers dead, survivors demanded higher wages and freedom, which weakened feudalism and led to uprisings such as the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

points.title: Magna Carta
points.brief: In 1215 English barons forced King John to agree that the king was also under the law, an early limit on a ruler's power.

points.title: Joan of Arc
points.brief: A peasant girl who said God sent her, Joan of Arc led French forces against the English in 1429, was burned in 1431, and became a French hero and saint.

points.title: What the Renaissance was
points.brief: The Renaissance, or rebirth, was a revival of Greek and Roman learning and art that began in Italian cities such as Florence in the 1400s.

points.title: Humanism
points.brief: Humanists studied ancient texts and believed people could improve themselves through learning, shifting attention from the next life to human achievement.

points.title: Patrons and the Medici
points.brief: Rich patrons such as the Medici banking family of Florence paid artists and scholars, using art to show their wealth and power.

points.title: Leonardo da Vinci
points.brief: Leonardo was a painter, inventor and scientist whose notebooks of anatomy and machines show the Renaissance idea of a person skilled in many fields.

points.title: The printing press
points.brief: Gutenberg's movable-type press, from about 1450, made books faster and cheaper, spreading ideas and helping the Reformation and science.

points.title: Longships and the Viking homeland
points.brief: Vikings came from Scandinavia, where farmland was scarce. Their light, fast longships could cross oceans and sail up shallow rivers.

points.title: Viking raids
points.brief: The raid on the monastery at Lindisfarne in 793 began centuries of attacks on rich, poorly defended places across the British Isles and Europe.

points.title: Viking traders and settlers
points.brief: Vikings also traded as far as Baghdad and settled in places such as Dublin, York, Normandy, Iceland and Greenland, reaching North America about 1000 CE.

points.title: Viking society and beliefs
points.brief: Society had jarls, free farmers and thralls, who were enslaved. A local assembly, the thing, settled disputes, and Vikings worshipped gods such as Odin and Thor.

points.title: The end of the Viking age
points.brief: As Scandinavian kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian, raiding faded. The defeat at Stamford Bridge in 1066 is often taken as its end.

points.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
points.brief: In 1206 Temujin united the nomadic Mongol tribes and took the title Genghis Khan, promoting followers for loyalty and skill rather than family.

points.title: How the Mongols conquered
points.brief: Mongol armies of mounted archers moved fast, used clever tactics and terror, and built the largest land empire in history.

points.title: Trade under the Mongols
points.brief: The Mongols kept the Silk Road safe and ran a relay postal system, so goods, ideas and travellers such as Marco Polo moved across Asia.

points.title: Kublai Khan and the empire's decline
points.brief: Kublai Khan conquered China and founded the Yuan dynasty, but the empire split into rival khanates, and the Yuan fell in 1368.

points.title: The emperor and the shogun
points.brief: From 1192 the shogun, a military ruler, held real power in Japan, while the emperor kept a religious and ceremonial role.

points.title: Samurai and bushido
points.brief: Samurai were warriors who served a lord, a daimyo, and followed bushido, a code of loyalty, honour and self-discipline.

points.title: Japan's social order
points.brief: Under the shoguns, society was ranked as samurai, then peasants, craftworkers and merchants, with the emperor and nobles above.

points.title: Uniting Japan
points.brief: After a century of civil war, Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu united Japan, and the Tokugawa shogunate began in 1603.

points.title: Japan closes its borders
points.brief: The Tokugawa shoguns banned Christianity and limited foreign trade to a few ports, giving Japan over 200 years of peace and isolation.

points.title: The end of the shoguns
points.brief: American warships under Perry forced Japan to open to trade in 1853, and in 1868 the Meiji Restoration ended rule by shoguns.
